extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical; includes Supplemental Information referenced but not in the text file)
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (2,898 lines, printed pages 941-962, including all tables, footnotes 1-33 and the reference list) in six chunks; nothing skipped. Metadata hint confirmed from the text (title, authors, APSR 113(4), pp. 941-962, DOI all match). Paul's markup: no markup files were among the input set ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty and no highlights, underlines or sticky notes were read. Plain-text extraction drops figure images, so Figures 1-3 values come from the printed notes and prose. Table 3 group averages do not extract cleanly (Panel B pitch-difference column is garbled), so only the t-tests and text figures are relied on. The paper contains no lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation or vote-share-of-election analysis; the only election-related material is the literature review on voter responses to candidate pitch.
extraction.research_question: Do small within-speaker deviations in vocal pitch (mean F0 relative to a speaker's own baseline) measure legislators' emotional intensity on an issue? Test case: do female House members speak with higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, compared with (a) male MCs on the same topic and (b) their own speech on other topics? Secondary questions: does pitch track issue commitments (women's interest-group scores; party-owned issues), and do emotionally intense female speeches about women relate to male MCs' subsequent speech and voting (p. 941-942, 944, 951)?
extraction.theory: Emotional arousal tightens the vocal folds and raises pitch (Puts, Gaulin and Verdolini 2006; Owren and Bachorowski 2007; Mauss and Robinson 2009) (p. 942). Pitch is a measure of arousal/intensity, not valence (fn 1). Because pitch is hard to control, it sits low on the "leakage hierarchy" (Zuckerman and Driver 1985; Ekman et al. 1991; Kraut 1978), so it is a less strategic signal than topic choice, word choice or speech length (p. 942-944). Descriptive representation theory: female legislators have experience-based commitment to women's concerns (Reingold 1992; Mansbridge 1999), so their intensity should rise when speaking about women (p. 944-945). Signalling extension: when many women speak intensely about women, male colleagues attend and respond (Boyd, Epstein and Martin 2010; Mendelberg, Karpowitz and Oliphant 2014), with a possible backlash alternative (Kathlene 1994; Krook 2015) (p. 951, 957). Partisan extension: parties own issues and partisans speak with more intensity on owned issues (Petrocik 1996; Petrocik, Benoit and Hansen 2003) (p. 949-951).
extraction.data: Source: HouseLive (Office of the Clerk) video, audio and closed-caption text for all US House floor debates, 6,432 hours from 863 debates, 2009-01-06 to 2014-08-04 (p. 944). Unit of analysis: individual floor speech of at least 50 words; N = 74,158 speeches (p. 944). Speaker sex from GovTrack; race, seniority, DW-NOMINATE and party from GovTrack/Voteview; committee chair from Stewart and Woon (2016) (p. 946). Table 1 model N: 74,151 speeches and 619 MCs (Models 1.1-1.2); 71,198 speeches and 613 MCs (Models 1.3-1.4). Female-speech counts: 13,484 speeches by women (2,403 mention women, 17.82%); 60,667 by men (5,507 mention women, 9.08%) (p. 946). Women's own speech, male-on-female-day analysis: 50,235 speeches, 509 men (Table 5). Male pitch analysis: 49,914 speeches, 506 men (Table 6). Voting analysis: 21,920 observations, 485 men (Table 7). Interest groups: 24 women's groups via Project Vote Smart, averaged per MC (p. 948). Women's bills: Volden, Wiseman and Wittmer (2018); CQ "Bills to Watch" count (p. 952). Closed captions reported ~95% accurate by the vendor; authors' transcription of 100 speeches matched (fn 11).
extraction.method: Pitch: mean fundamental frequency per speech extracted with Praat (Boersma 1993 algorithm; male floor 75 Hz, ceiling 300 Hz; female range 100-500 Hz), then z-scored within speaker so units are SD above/below each MC's baseline (p. 945-946; alternative Praat windows in SI S22-S30). Topic: binary indicator for any term in Pearson and Dancey (2011b) women dictionary; alternatives are word-share and a 30-topic structural topic model (STM) (p. 945-946). Models: multilevel logit for "Women mentioned" (Models 1.1-1.2, 5.1-5.2) and multilevel linear regression for standardized pitch with random intercepts per MC (Models 1.3-1.4, 4.x, 6.x); outcome models for Table 5, 6, 7 are multilevel logit/linear with day-level Female Speeches, Female Pitch and interactions (p. 946-956). Descriptive comparisons: Welch-type t-tests across speakers and groups (Table 2; Table 3 top-25 vs bottom-25 female MCs by pitch difference; t = 2.59, df = 48). Partisan issue test: Table 4 interaction of party with party-owned STM topics. Male voting outcome: proportion of votes cast with female speakers, standardized against each male MC's prior co-voting rate (p. 955-956). Predicted values from Models 5.2, 6.1 and 7.2 at female pitch +/-2 SD (p. 953-956).
extraction.identification: None causal. The paper states the design is observational and that "legislators' speeches on women simply cannot be randomly assigned" (p. 957). Within-speaker z-scoring removes stable speaker-level pitch differences (including sex differences in baseline pitch), random intercepts absorb unobserved MC heterogeneity, and a rich control set is used (race, seniority, chair, DW-NOMINATE, party, one-minute speech, duration, election year). Placebo tests and dyadic models are in SI S55-S62. Male-response models restrict to men who spoke on the same legislative day as women's speeches and add agenda controls (Women's bills, CQ bills). The volume-times-pitch interaction is the key test. Robustness: results unchanged under alternative DV operationalizations (word share, STM) (p. 946), re-estimated without observations beyond +/-2 SD (fn 28, p. 953), and different Praat pitch windows (p. 945-946).
extraction.scope: Population: all US House floor speeches of at least 50 words during the 111th-113th Congresses (Jan 2009 to Aug 2014), roughly 77-81 women in the House in that span (p. 956). Institution: US House floor only (not the Senate, committees, or state legislatures, which the authors name as future audio sources, p. 958). Era: 2009-2014. Speeches are natural floor speech, not acted or induced emotion (p. 944). The authors explicitly do not claim general causal effects of women's speech on male behavior (p. 957).
measures: Standardized mean F0 (vocal pitch) per speech, in SD above/below speaker baseline (Praat; Titze 2000 F0 framework)
Raw mean F0 in Hz (Table 2 and footnote 15)
Women-mention dictionary indicator (Pearson and Dancey 2011b), with word-share and STM alternatives
Female (GovTrack sex)
Party, DW-NOMINATE, seniority, committee chair, race, one-minute speech, speech duration, election year

key_findings.finding: Women are more likely than men to reference women in floor speeches.
key_findings.numbers: 17.82% of female speeches (2,403/13,484) vs 9.08% of male speeches (5,507/60,667); predicted probability 0.17 vs 0.08 (2.13 times). Holds with controls (Model 1.2).

key_findings.finding: Female MCs speak at higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, and male MCs do not.
key_findings.numbers: Female x 'Women mentioned' = 0.090 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) without controls and 0.112 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) with controls. Female MCs: +0.09 SD when referencing women, about five times the male change of +0.02 SD. Male pitch unchanged (t = 0.02, df 58,281). Democratic women t = 3.12; Republican women t = 2.81.

key_findings.finding: Raw pitch levels: female MCs' pitch rises on speeches mentioning women; male pitch is flat.
key_findings.numbers: Female MCs: 206.01 Hz when mentioning women vs 203.27 Hz otherwise. Male MCs: 151.50 Hz vs 151.49 Hz. Republican women 207.02 Hz vs Democratic women 205.68 Hz when mentioning women (not significantly different, fn 15).

key_findings.finding: Among female MCs, the most emotionally intense on women's issues have higher women's interest-group scores.
key_findings.numbers: Top 25 vs bottom 25 female MCs by pitch difference: difference in Vote Smart scores t = 2.59, df = 48, p < 0.02. Democratic women only: t = 2.83, df = 39, p <= 0.01. Republican women: t = 0.14, df = 7, not significant (small N). Table 3 group averages are not reliably extracted and are not relied on.

key_findings.finding: Partisans speak with higher pitch on their party-owned issues and lower pitch on the opposing party's issues.
key_findings.numbers: Democrat x Democratic-owned issues = 0.328 (Model 4.1) and 0.288 (Model 4.2), both p<0.01. Republican x Republican-owned issues = 0.380 (Model 4.3) and 0.355 (Model 4.4), both p<0.01. Democrats use 9.02% more words on Democratic-owned topics; Republicans use 17.21% more on Republican-owned topics (t = 18.43 and 30.51). Topic shares capture under 8% of words per speech on average.

key_findings.finding: Male MCs mention women more often on days with more female speeches on women, and more so when female pitch is high in the interaction model.
key_findings.numbers: Table 5 Model 5.2: Female speeches = 0.060 (SE 0.003); Female speeches x Female pitch = 0.011 (p<0.05). Figure 1 (Female pitch +2 SD): going from 0 to 43 female speeches raises P(male mention of women) from 0.05 to 0.56. From 6 to 11 speeches (1 SD either side of mean): 0.07 to 0.10. Model 5.1 interaction is not significant at 0.05.

key_findings.finding: Male MCs' pitch on women rises with the volume and intensity of female speeches on women.
key_findings.numbers: Three-way interaction (Women mentioned x Female speeches x Female pitch) = 0.016 (SE 0.005, p<0.01). At Female pitch +2 SD, raising female speeches from 6 to 11 moves male pitch on women from 0.17 SD to 0.26 SD; from 0 to 43 moves it from 0.12 SD to 1.79 SD.

key_findings.finding: Male co-voting with female speakers rises with the volume and intensity of women's speeches; no backlash detected.
key_findings.numbers: Female speeches x Female pitch = 0.015 (Model 7.1, p<0.01) and 0.012 (Model 7.2, SE 0.002, p<0.01). At Female pitch +2 SD, the standardized co-voting rate rises from -0.23 SD to +0.53 SD as female speeches go from 0 to 43 (p. 956). Authors read this as no evidence of male backlash (p. 957).

key_findings.finding: The maximum observed volume of female speeches on women is large relative to the chamber.
key_findings.numbers: 43 female speeches on women on one day = 56% of the 77-81 women in the 111th-113th Congresses.

key_findings.finding: Results are robust to alternative outcome measures and to trimming extreme pitch values.
key_findings.location: p. 946 (alternative DVs); fn 28, p. 953 (+/-2 SD trim); SI S30-S36, S66-S69
key_findings.numbers: Word-share and STM operationalizations of women-topic give identical substantive results. Trimming pitch beyond +/-2 SD is 'generally robust' (no numbers reported in text).

limitations: Observational design; the authors say they do not claim causal effects of female MCs' intense speech on male behavior, and that alternative explanations cannot be ruled out (p. 957).
Male response is not zero at low female participation: at few female speeches the effect is absent or negative, so the signalling story is conditional on volume (p. 957).
Backlash is examined only with one voting measure and cannot be ruled out in other outcomes; votes may come before or after speeches because the data have no time stamps (fn 31, p. 955-956).
Pitch-based intensity is an arousal measure, not valence; a single pitch number cannot say whether a speaker is enthusiastic or angry (fn 1, p. 942).
Mean F0 per speech is a coarse measure; other factors (question intonation, duration) also move mean pitch, though controls are included (fn 8, p. 945; p. 958-959).
Women-topic is a coarse dictionary indicator; alternatives used as robustness checks (p. 945-946).
Effect size is small: 0.09 SD for female MCs on women's topics, which the authors concede is 'slight' and likely below conscious control (p. 947).
Confidence and expertise could explain some intensity; the paper does not separate them, and male MCs with the most women's bills did not show the same pattern (fn 19, p. 948).

Republican-owned and Republican-women effects are weaker or not significant in some specifications, partly due to small N of Republican women (p. 948-949; fn 17; t = 0.14 with df = 7 for Republican women in Table 3 comparison).
Male MCs' floor attendance is unobserved; the sample uses all male MCs who spoke the same day as a proxy for exposure (fn 24, p. 953).
Closed-caption text is ~95% accurate per the vendor (fn 11, p. 945).
Table 3 group averages do not extract cleanly from the PDF text; only the reported t-tests are used here.
Single chamber (US House) and single era (2009-2014); generalization to other chambers or periods is untested (p. 958-959).

summary_md:
Dietrich, Hayes and O'Brien use 74,158 US House floor speeches from 2009 to 2014, each at least 50 words, taken from Clerk HouseLive audio. They measure each speech's mean vocal pitch (F0, extracted with Praat) and z-score it against the speaker's own baseline. They argue this is a hard-to-fake measure of arousal. It tracks intensity, not valence (footnote 1). Female members speak about 0.09 to 0.11 SD above their baseline when they mention women, while male members do not change (Table 1). Partisans speak about 0.29 to 0.38 SD higher on topics their party owns (Table 4). On days when many women speak with high pitch about women, male members mention women more, raise their own pitch on the topic, and co-vote more with the women speakers (Tables 5-7). These response results are observational, and the authors say they are not causal (p. 957).

The system has already built this method. `fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:209-254` cites the paper by name and computes `pitch_deviation_from_speaker_baseline_z` and `topic_emotional_intensity`. The two differ in three ways. The paper relies on a cross-speaker contrast (female versus male, times topic) and roughly 120 speeches per speaker. The system reports a per-speaker topic mean with no comparison group. Its floors are 5 speech units per member, 2 topics, and 2 units per topic (`fec/audio_rules.py:20-22`). Effects of 0.1 to 0.4 SD cannot be detected at those floors. With only two topics, the sign of each topic's deviation is fixed by construction. The paper also measures in one floor venue with one channel. The system's baseline is pooled across interview programs and channels. The paper supports the system's existing rules: absolute F0 stays out of personality scores, and audio stays display-only. It also points to a better identity source: Clerk floor video, where the chamber has already identified the speaker.

bearings.paper_claim: Intensity is each speech's mean F0 z-scored against the speaker's own baseline, in SD units. Table 1 pitch models (N1 = 74,151 speeches, N2 = 619 members, 2009-2014 House floor): female x 'women' mentioned = 0.090 (SE 0.027) without controls and 0.112 (SE 0.027) with controls. About 120 speeches per member is only the average (74,151 / 619); the paper states no required sample size. The authors call the raw magnitude 'slight enough'.
bearings.paper_location: p. 945-947, Table 1 (pitch models); p. 947
bearings.system_side: Candidate descriptor converts eGeMAPS semitones to Hz (code comment cites Dietrich, Hayes and O'Brien at line 210), z-scores each speech unit against the member mean and SD inside _speaker_pitch_profile, and reports topic_emotional_intensity as mean deviation per transcript topic. Floors: 5 speech units per member, 2 distinct topics, 2 units per reported topic. No comparison group. Default status CANDIDATE_CONSUMED_BY_NOTHING_AWAITING_USER_RATIFICATION (line 273). The brain's count of 0 accepted v2 clips was not checked.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:209-254 (comment line 210; standardization and topic summary); fec/audio_rules.py:20-22 (floors 5 / 2 / 2)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The within-speaker z transform transfers. The inference does not: the paper identifies effects from a cross-speaker contrast over 74,151 speeches, while the system computes one member's topic mean from 2-5 units. Assuming independent units, the SE of a 2-5 unit topic mean is about 0.45-0.7 SD (arithmetic; no minimum detectable effect was computed). The paper's effects are 0.09-0.38 SD.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 1 numbers, the standardization and the floors are confirmed in code and text. Softened: the paper does not say a member needs about 120 speeches; that figure is an average. The power statement is arithmetic under an independence assumption, not a computed detection threshold.

bearings.paper_claim: Pitch measures arousal, not valence (footnote 1, p. 942). The paper adds controls for speech duration, a one-minute dummy and an election-year dummy (p. 946, Table 1). It acknowledges that question intonation also moves mean F0 (footnote 8, p. 945) but does not control for it, arguing mean pitch remains reliable. The baseline is one venue: the House floor via HouseLive.

Neither the per-member z nor the Washington Journal subject_effects centering has a duration, question or speech-type term. The WJ table on the desk shows topic shifts from as few as 2 reactions. The brain channel note was not checked.

bearings.paper_claim: Raw F0 differs mainly by sex: Table 2 gives female means of about 203-206 Hz and male means of about 151 Hz. Deviation from each speaker's own baseline removes stable between-speaker level by construction. The authors read the measure as an emotional disposition toward an issue, and say the slight changes are consistent with pitch indicating a lawmaker's emotional disposition toward an issue.

The brain's sex-confound correlation (r = -0.266) and the audio-N MISS at N = 90 are brain-sourced and were not checked.

The paper gives no evidence that pitch measures a between-member disposition such as N, so the closed audio-N route is consistent with it. The paper's own gloss is a topic-specific emotional disposition, which the rel calls a state; it is an interpretation the authors do not test.

Softened: the paper frames the measure as a disposition toward issues and leaves room for a trait-like reading, so 'a topic-level state, not a trait' overstates what the paper establishes. bearings.paper_claim: Speech topic, word choice and length of remarks are highly controllable and driven by strategic concerns, while vocal pitch typically lies beyond the individual's control, making it a more honest indicator of intensity on a given issue (leakage hierarchy, pp. 942-944). The paper does not compare dictionary tone or LSD scores with pitch.
bearings.paper_location: p. 942-944 (leakage hierarchy passage)
bearings.system_side: Press intensity is |LSD net| / words or (pos + neg) / words (lsd_charge) per member press release. The press pillar multiplies stance sign by this heat.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A theoretical argument only; the paper never tests LSD tone against pitch. The claim that press releases are staff-drafted and so more strategic than floor speech has no support in the paper or the code. LSD charge measures crafted rhetorical tone, not felt intensity, and should be labelled that way.
bearings.verifier_note: The leakage passage and code lines are confirmed. Softened: the paper says pitch is less controllable, not that audio gives an intensity signal that text cannot give. The staff-drafting claim is unsupported here.

summary_issues: Sample and denominator: summary gives 74,158 speeches; Table 1 models use N1 = 74,151 speeches and 619 members. Both figures should name their window (2009-2014, House floor) and denominator.
'Hard-to-fake' is not the paper's term. The paper says pitch is difficult for speakers to control (abstract; p. 942).
'About 120 speeches per speaker' is an average (74,151 / 619), not a design parameter or a stated requirement.
'Male members mention women more' holds only in Table 5 Model 5.2 (interaction 0.011, p < 0.05); Model 5.1 is 0.009 and not significant.
'Raise their own pitch on the topic' rests on the three-way term in Table 6 (0.016, p < 0.01). The 'women mentioned' main effect is 0.026 and not significant.

meta.title: Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting

extraction.title: Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting
extraction.document_type: empirical research article: two randomized survey experiments, with a calibration phase run on previously collected experimental data
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks (1249 lines, 80770 bytes): pp. 1-10 including abstract, intro, Study 1 and Study 2 results, Fig 1-3 captions and axis labels, Discussion, Materials and Methods, and references. Page images unavailable. Paul markup: no annotation files exist (n_annots 0, annot_sha12s empty), so paul_markup is empty and 0 items were dropped. Not a Paul research note. Metadata hints verified correct. Fig 2 profile-level numbers appear only as unlabelled values in the text dump and are not mapped to profiles. SI not provided.
extraction.research_question: Does political microtargeting (message pretesting combined with machine learning, so each person sees the message predicted to persuade them most) produce a persuasive advantage over a naive random-message strategy and a single-best-message strategy? Does targeting by more covariates, or targeting issues rather than messages on one issue, add returns?
extraction.theory: Microtargeting depends on treatment effect heterogeneity, meaning different people respond differently to different messages. Large-scale studies (refs 24-27) find heterogeneity usually small, so the persuasive returns to microtargeting are theoretically ambiguous. Study 2 frames the choice: if people are most persuadable on the same issues, show everyone one issue message; if persuadability differs across people by issue, targeting issues pays.
extraction.data: Study 1 calibration: two existing survey experiments (ref 37). U.S. Citizenship Act (n=17,013; 26 pro-Act treatment messages plus control) and universal basic income (n=6,408; 10 anti-UBI treatment messages plus control). Study 2 calibration: first experiment of ref 38 (n=3,990 U.S. respondents; 9,712 observations; 36 policy issues; 48 professionally produced progressive video ads from the Peoria Project database). Experimental phase: new U.S. adult sample recruited through Lucid in Feb 2022, quota-matched on age, gender, ethnicity and region; 7,531 entered, 5,284 analyzed (completed at least one module). Three modules in random order. Unit: individual respondent. Outcome: policy support (Study 1, same items as calibration) or 5-point agreement with message position (Study 2, message-specific). Per-module N not stated in main text. Preregistered (osf.io/kvd9t). Data on OSF (osf.io/t3dhe).
extraction.method: Calibration: for each covariate profile (255 profiles from 8 covariates in Study 1; 511 profiles from 9 covariates in Study 2), generalized random forests (grf R package) trained on 75 percent of data estimate message-level heterogeneity. The message predicted best for each subgroup is evaluated on the 25 percent test set by restricting the treatment group to people assigned their predicted-best message and comparing to control. Monte Carlo cross-validation: 250 random splits; median per profile; top profile in each stratum (1, 2-3, or 4+ covariates) refit on full data. Single-best-message = message with largest OLS ATE in training data. Experimental phase: OLS with condition dummies vs control, robust (HC2) SEs. Study 2: separate OLS per strategy, then difference-in-differences interaction models.
extraction.identification: Randomized survey experiment. Condition assignment is independent of pretreatment covariates by design, so filtering the treatment group to predicted-best assignment preserves covariate balance in expectation. Targeting covariates were measured before treatment. Study 1 microtargeting arm further randomized across three covariate profiles with equal probability. Study 2 randomizes strategy first, then treatment vs control within strategy. Balance and attrition checks reported in SI (not reviewed).
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. adults recruited online (quota-matched), February 2022. Issues: U.S. Citizenship Act, universal basic income, and 36 multi-issue advocacy topics (e.g., net neutrality, minimum wage, gun control, climate change). Setting: issue advocacy and ideology-shift campaigns; messages delivered by survey video, not field advertising. Era: calibration data from prior survey work; experimental data 2022; publication 2023.
measures: Persuasive impact = difference in policy support (percentage points) between treatment and control, by strategy
Study 2 outcome: 5-point Likert agreement with the message position, specific to each message
Study 1 covariates: age, gender, party ID, ideology (binned), religiosity (1-7), three moral-foundation scores (MF1-MF3) from 12 Moral Foundations Questionnaire items via PCA
Study 2 covariates: age, gender, party ID, ideology, education, race, income, Cognitive Reflection Test (0-4), political knowledge test (0-4)
Exploratory: issue importance and willingness to share the video with a friend or colleague

key_findings.finding: Study 1, U.S. Citizenship Act: microtargeting produced over twice the persuasive impact of single-best-message, and far more than naive messaging.
Study 1, UBI: microtargeting point estimates favor it over both alternatives but are not statistically significant.
Study 1 precision-weighted across both modules: microtargeting advantage is about 70 percent larger than SBM and over 200 percent larger than naive.

No evidence that targeting by more covariates increases persuasive returns; the advantage was qualitatively largest with one covariate, though differences were slight. Coarse targeting by party or ideology alone produced an advantage.
key_findings.numbers: Fig 2 profile values not mapped in text; differences described as relatively slight

key_findings.finding: Study 2, multi-issue: microtargeting is directionally but not significantly below single-best-message, and clearly above naive messaging.
key_findings.location: p.6, Study 2 Experimental Phase; Fig 3, p.6

key_findings.finding: Study 2 conclusion: targeting different issues to different people was not more impactful than distributing one pretested ad on one issue to everyone, though pretested targeting clearly beat naive.
Messages predicted most persuasive in Study 2 often dealt with obscure policies (e.g., net neutrality), consistent with low-information issues being most persuadable.
Study 1 headline advantage (70 percent or more) was driven primarily by the U.S. Citizenship Act messaging.
key_findings.numbers: 70 percent or more over alternatives

key_findings.finding: Authors find no evidence that the microtargeting advantage requires vast personal data; a single covariate was enough to generate the benefit observed.
Authors conclude the advantage of microtargeting is highly context dependent, with clear gains in a policy-centered campaign and limited gains in a multi-issue campaign.

limitations: Survey, not field, experiments: covariates measured precisely and exposure forced. Authors say this may overstate the advantage because campaigns lack high-quality covariates and mis-targeting may reduce efficacy (p.7).
Social media ad delivery is nonrandom and idiosyncratic and may attenuate the advantage; engagement optimization might boost it (p.7).
Forced exposure: respondents engaged with content they might have ignored in real life; roughly half of disseminated political ads may not reach intended audiences (p.7, citing ref 49).
Only a small set of low-salience issues and messages; high-salience contexts with countermessaging likely yield smaller effects and possibly a smaller relative advantage (p.7).
U.S. only; candidate-centered campaigns and non-U.S. contexts untested (p.7).
Cost-effectiveness not assessed; microtargeting needs more time, money and data science than SBM, which could yield more persuasion per dollar (p.8).

Study 2 divergence unresolved: pretest design was mixed between and within subjects, calibration preceded follow-up by almost a year, and all Study 2 messages were progressive professional videos (p.5, p.8).
Study 1 excluded messages opposing the Act and supporting UBI due to resource constraints (p.9).
Well-funded campaigns could train models at finer covariate resolution with larger pretest data, so results may understate the advantage (p.7).
Per-module experimental N and balance/attrition checks are in SI, not the main text (p.9); SI not reviewed.
Study 2 outcome variables differ by message, so strategy comparisons rely on a difference-in-differences design (p.9).

summary_md: Tappin, Wittenberg, Hewitt, Berinsky and Rand (PNAS 2023) test whether microtargeting, meaning pretesting messages and using generalized random forests to send each covariate profile the message predicted to persuade it most, beats two simpler strategies: random messages (naive) and one pretested best message for everyone (single-best-message, SBM). In a Feb 2022 Lucid sample (5,284 U.S. adults analyzed), Study 1 on a single policy found microtargeting moved support 5.96 pp vs 3.48 SBM and 1.79 naive (precision-weighted over two modules). Almost all of that came from the Citizenship Act module (5.17 vs 2.41). The UBI module was not significant. Targeting on one covariate, such as party or ideology alone, did as well as targeting on two to four or more. In Study 2, across 36 issues, letting the targeted issue vary by person did not beat one best issue ad (12.30 vs 15.42, P=0.11), though both beat naive (6.19). The authors call the advantage highly context dependent. They say forced-exposure survey estimates probably overstate field returns, and they did not test candidate races. For Paul's systems, the closest point of contact is Terrier's Untapped potential score. It ranks whom to contact by support closeness to 0.5, chance of voting and sphere of influence. It has no message dimension and no estimate of effect size. The paper says message choice changes the effect a lot (naive was near zero in one module) and that coarse partisan targeting is enough to capture the gain. That is an extension Terrier could add cheaply, but only through its own pretest. Melange's legislator-side persuadability is barely touched: this is a mass-public survey study. Its relevance there is limited to context on low-information issues. No brain rule is in conflict.

bearings.paper_claim: Study 1 (Lucid, Feb 2022; 5,284 analyzed across both modules). Citizenship Act: microtargeting 5.17 pp vs single-best-message 2.41 vs naive random message -0.96 (P=0.016 and P<0.001). Precision-weighted across both modules: 5.96 vs 3.48 vs 1.79. UBI module: microtargeting 7.16 vs single-best-message 5.03 vs naive 5.70, not significant. Profiles were ranked with generalized random forests (grf R package) over 250 Monte Carlo 75/25 splits. The advantage was qualitatively largest for one-covariate targeting, though differences were slight.

bearings.system_side: Untapped potential ranks each person by (wp x (1-|2s-1|) x t + (1-wp) x s x (1-t)) x (1 + wi x i), with module defaults wp=0.5 and wi=0.5 that a district can override. It chooses whom to contact, not what to say. It has no message or script variant and no effect-size term, and the (1-|2s-1|) term peaks at s=0.5 by construction.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Tappin's effects are online survey estimates from Feb 2022 U.S. respondents with forced exposure on low-salience policy attitudes. They are not field or door-canvass effects. The paper says candidate-centered and non-U.S. settings are untested, and it says survey estimates may overstate the relative advantage of microtargeting in the field. A party or ideology split is the coarse covariate the paper found sufficient in-sample, and Terrier holds registration and partisan scores. Any gain stays UNVERIFIED until Terrier runs its own pretest.

extraction.venue: Political Analysis 34: 312-328 (published online 30 January 2026; open access)
extraction.document_type: Journal article (methods paper with applications; replication code on Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/K3I16E and GitHub)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 853 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\ca7a80494661.txt, including the abstract, Sections 1-5, Tables 1-3, Figures 1-4 captions and content, footnotes, and the reference list. extraction.research_question: Can audio be made usable as data for political research, given the "alignment crisis" (large text and audio corpora that do not intersect at the utterance level), and which audio features (LLDs, MFCCs, learned embeddings) and classifiers are useful for speech characterization, speaker identification, and emotion/valence measurement? The paper is a methods-and-applications demonstration; it does not test a substantive hypothesis.
extraction.theory: No formal theory is tested. The framing draws on the text-as-data literature (Grimmer and Stewart 2013; Wilkerson and Casas 2017) and on the claim that nonverbal audio cues (pitch, energy, intonation) carry political meaning not captured by transcripts (Section 2; Klofstad 2016; Dietrich et al. 2019; Damann, Knox and Lucas 2025). Emotion is treated as socially and politically constructed (Section 4.4, p.325), so classifier outputs are framed as starting points, not measures of emotion.
extraction.data: Unit: utterance/sentence within televised U.S. presidential and vice-presidential debates. Period: 1960 to 2020 (first televised debate 1960; 2020 included). Videos: 45 (243,023 s = 4,050 min = 67.5 h). Transcripts: 47,150 sentences (38,649 from candidates; 8,501 from moderators, panelists, or audience), originally from the USElecDeb60To16 dataset (Haddadan, Cabrio and Villata 2020), taken from the Commission on Presidential Debates site and extended to 2020, with some sentence omissions fixed (Section 4, p.317). Participants: 34 candidates (16 Democrat, 15 Republican, 3 independent), 82 moderators/panelists, 59 audience members. Video source: Commission on Presidential Debates YouTube channel. Note for the record: the speaker-identification section (Section 4.3, p.321) reports 44,559 sentences and 156 speakers, which does not reconcile with the 47,150 sentence count in Section 1 (p.314); the paper does not explain the gap. Forced-alignment validation used a random subset of 500 utterances, each rated five times by crowd annotators (p.318). Emotion models were applied to the debates; their training corpora were IEMOCAP (about 12 h of acted and improvised audio, Busso et al. 2008) and MSP-Podcast v1.7 (about 84 h, Lotfian and Busso 2019).
extraction.method: Four applications of increasing complexity (Section 4, Table 2). (1) Forced alignment: aeneas, which matches MFCCs of the audio to synthetic-voice MFCCs via dynamic time warping; validated by human ratings on a 1-5 scale. (2) Speech characterization: pYIN pitch (F0) in 32 ms rolling windows and RMS energy per utterance, normalized by each debate's average loudness; within-speaker pitch deviations averaged over 5 s windows (Figure 3c). (3) Speaker identification: a custom CNN on MFCCs (two blocks of convolution, max-pooling and dropout) versus a single-layer neural network on 768-dimensional wav2vec2-base embeddings (Hugging Face facebook/wav2vec2-base); Adam, learning rate 0.001, cross-entropy loss, batch 32 (MFCC) or 8 (wav2vec2), early stopping with patience 3 (footnote 9). (4) Emotion: off-the-shelf models, not retrained: a SpeechBrain wav2vec2 model fine-tuned on IEMOCAP for four classes (anger, happiness, sadness, neutral), and Wagner et al. (2023) dimensional models for arousal, dominance and valence trained on MSP-Podcast. Text-based emotion and sentiment classifiers are compared with audio-based labels as a cross-check (Figure 4d).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is a measurement and feasibility paper. Validation is by human crowd ratings for alignment (Section 4.1), held-out test accuracy for speaker identification (Table 3), and reported third-party benchmark accuracy/CCC for emotion models (Section 4.4). The paper explicitly says cross-speaker comparisons are confounded by microphone placement, compression, and sampling (p.320), and recommends within-speaker shifts or speaker-dependent human validation (p.324).
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. presidential and vice-presidential general-election debates, 1960-2020, all televised debate audio available on the CPD YouTube channel. Institution: candidate-moderator debate format, not legislatures. The paper argues the LLD and MFCC features are language-agnostic, but wav2vec2 embeddings and the emotion models are trained on specific languages and corpora and may not generalize across languages, accents, or cultures (Sections 3.3 and 5, pp.316, 326). Alignment and ASR context also draws on parliamentary data (UK Hansard/ParliamentTV, German Bundestag work) only in the literature review.

key_findings.finding: MFCC-based forced alignment of audio to transcripts performs well on crowd ratings; about 5% of text-audio pairs were rated not aligned at all, and short or interrupted sentences drove the poor alignment.
key_findings.numbers: 500 utterances, 5 annotations each; percentage agreement (PA) 85.26%; distance-based agreement (DA) 95.76%; about 5% rated 1 (not aligned at all).

key_findings.finding: Pitch extraction ranks candidates by average F0. Women candidates (Palin, Harris, Clinton) appear among the top five; the bottom five include Reagan, Lieberman, Edwards, Cheney and Dole. Pitch-based comparisons are presented as exploratory and confounded by recording conditions.
key_findings.numbers: 34 candidates; top five by average pitch include three of the four women candidates in the sample (Ferraro ranked sixth).

key_findings.finding: Normalized energy differs most across the two debates involving women candidates. Palin and Ferraro had lower average energy than their opponents (Biden, H.W. Bush).
key_findings.numbers: Energy normalized by each debate's average loudness; largest energy gaps appear in the Palin-Biden and Ferraro-Bush debates (no effect size reported).

key_findings.finding: Within-speaker pitch variation is far higher in 2020 than in the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debate, which the authors link to changing norms and technology but do not test.
key_findings.numbers: Comparison of 1960 and 2020 first debates, normalized to each speaker's own baseline, averaged over 5-s windows; no statistic reported.

key_findings.finding: Wav2vec2 embeddings substantially outperform MFCCs for speaker identification, and the gap widens as the number of speaker classes grows.
key_findings.numbers: Individual debates: MFCC 0.888 (+/-0.085) vs wav2vec2 0.974 (+/-0.024). All 156 speakers: MFCC 0.081 vs wav2vec2 0.914 (table 0.08103 vs 0.913568). Candidates only, 34 labels: MFCC 0.134 vs wav2vec2 0.946.

key_findings.finding: Off-the-shelf emotion models label a large share of utterances as angry, with most of the rest neutral; sad and happy are rare. The authors say the four-label scheme is too simple.
key_findings.numbers: Reported IEMOCAP four-class test accuracy of 75.3%; no per-debate figures given in text beyond the plotted percentages.

key_findings.finding: Candidates with higher pitch (Clinton, Kemp) also score as more angry, and low-pitch candidates (Cheney, Lieberman) score as calmer. The paper says these contradict expert coding of Trump, who is not among the top angry candidates in the model output.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, p.323, Figure 4b; contradiction cites Bucy et al. 2020
key_findings.numbers: Bucy et al. (2020) expert coding of the 2016 Trump-Clinton debate: Trump anger/threatening tone 82.6% of interventions vs Clinton 35.3%.

key_findings.finding: Dominance-arousal profiles place Clinton, Perot and Anderson at high dominance and high arousal; Lieberman and Cheney are lowest on both. No candidate stands out on valence.
key_findings.numbers: Model CCC for arousal 0.744, dominance 0.655, valence 0.638 (reported for the Wagner et al. 2023 model on MSP-Podcast, p.323).

key_findings.finding: Audio-based emotion labels and text-based labels only partly agree. Text emotion models mostly output neutral, while the audio model is more differentiated. Anger co-occurs with negative sentiment in 32% of cases.
key_findings.numbers: Anger-negative sentiment co-occurrence 32% (as reported in text).

limitations: Forced alignment is poor for very short or interrupted sentences (Figure 2b; p.318).

Cross-speaker and cross-time comparisons of pitch and energy are confounded by microphone placement, audio compression, sampling, and recording technology (pp.319-320, 324). The paper explicitly warns against naive interpretation.
Emotion and valence outputs are not validated against human coding of these debates; the authors call for speaker-dependent human validation (p.324).
Emotion classifiers can encode and amplify gender, ethnicity and vocal bias, possibly labeling women as angry when using neutral or assertive tones (pp.324-325).
Four-label emotion categories are simplistic (p.324). Emotion definitions vary across individuals, circumstances and cultures (p.322).
Training corpora (IEMOCAP, MSP-Podcast) are not debates; out-of-domain generalization is assumed from reported benchmarks, not tested here (p.322).
Embeddings are language-specific and computationally expensive for typical researchers; MFCC/LLD features are language-agnostic but less accurate for complex tasks (pp.316, 326).
Only U.S. presidential and VP debates are studied; the authors note the need for comparative work outside the U.S. (p.322).
Copyright prevents sharing the videos; broadcasters gave contradictory answers on rights, and CBS quoted a licensing fee from $2,500 (footnote 4, p.314).
Data-protection and copyright concerns apply when audio is sent to external ASR APIs such as Google or YouTube (p.314, footnote 2).
Sentence count does not reconcile between Section 1 (47,150) and Section 4.3 (44,559); the paper does not explain the difference (pp.314, 321).
Reported ASR error rates (WER 0.03-0.26) come from prior lab-condition validations that do not account for noise or crosstalk (Proksch, Wratil and Wackerle 2019; p.314).
measures: Word error rate (WER) and match error rate (MER) (background, footnotes 1 and 3; cited figures from prior work)
Percentage agreement (PA) and distance-based agreement (DA) for alignment ratings (Supplementary Appendix D)
Pitch F0 via pYIN, 32 ms rolling windows (p.319)
Root-mean-squared energy, normalized by debate average loudness (p.319)
Classification test accuracy for speaker identification (Table 3)
Discrete emotion label percentages (angry, happy, neutral, sad) per debate and per candidate (Figure 4a-b)
Dominance, arousal and valence scores; concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) for model benchmarks (pp.322-323)
Co-occurrence matrices between audio emotion and text emotion/sentiment labels (Figure 4d)

summary_md:
Mestre and Ryan (Political Analysis 2026) is a methods paper on audio as data. Its corpus is 45 U.S. presidential and VP debate videos (1960-2020; 47,150 transcript sentences). It runs four demonstrations. (1) Aeneas MFCC/DTW forced alignment, rated by crowd workers on 500 utterances x 5 ratings: percentage agreement 85.26%, distance agreement 95.76%, and about 5% of pairs not aligned at all, mostly short or interrupted sentences. (2) pYIN pitch and RMS energy. Energy is normalized by each debate's loudness, and within-speaker pitch deviation is shown over time. (3) Closed-set speaker identification. A single layer on mean-pooled wav2vec2-base embeddings reaches 0.914 accuracy across 156 speakers; a CNN on MFCCs reaches 0.081. (4) Off-the-shelf emotion models. The authors say these are biased by gender and pitch, and they disagree with expert coding.

For Melange the paper is less outside evidence than a method source. The speaker-identity research layer already copies it closely: `b5_audio_neural_head.py` reproduces the wav2vec2/Adam/batch-8/patience-3 head and cites section 4.3 and footnote 9, and `b5_audio_align_turns.py` uses Aeneas as the paper does. Melange's run of that same method on congressional audio failed. The fresh-21 neural EER was .226, against a bar of 5% or less. That run split train and test by source and event and used weak caption labels. The paper's 0.914 is in-domain debate audio, where the authors themselves warn that microphone placement and compression confound comparisons across speakers. So the paper's accuracy is not a benchmark Melange should expect to reach. The paper also backs the within-speaker pitch design and the fix for the sex confound in pitch variability. It cautions against the cross-member pooled eGeMAPS z-scores, which have no per-recording loudness or channel control. Its warnings about emotion models support keeping audio display-only.

extraction.research_question: Can a "minimally-supervised" sentiment dictionary built from the corpus itself (seed words plus GloVe word-vector similarity) yield valid sentiment measures for specialized vocabularies where standard dictionaries (LIWC, AFINN) fail? The paper then applies the method to U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions to measure tone across 1792-2010, including over time and per justice.
extraction.theory: Distributional hypothesis: words used in similar contexts have similar meanings (p.4-5). Word vectors trained on a domain corpus place sentiment-laden words near seed words, so a small seed set grows a domain-appropriate dictionary. Standard dictionaries embed fixed valences that may be wrong in specialized contexts (e.g., "love" and "bagel" in tennis, p.3-4). Semantic drift over time is handled by re-estimating dictionaries on temporal subsets (p.19-20). The paper argues sentiment in court opinions is a substantive proxy for justices' disagreement and the norm of consensus (p.17-18).
extraction.data: Movie reviews (benchmark): Large Movie Review Dataset, 100,000 IMDB reviews (25,000 positive, 25,000 negative, 50,000 unlabeled). Word vectors were trained on 75,000 documents (12,500 positive, 12,500 negative, 50,000 unlabeled); 25,000 held-out test documents were used for an out-of-sample check (p.9-11). Mean review length 184 tokens, max 2,085 (p.13). Supreme Court: all cases 1792-2010 from justia.com, split into opinion-level files; only majority opinions retained; matched to the Supreme Court Database (Spaeth et al. 2012). About 26,000 unique majority opinions spanning 217 years (p.18-19). Mean majority opinion length 2,097 tokens. Justice-level analyses cover justices with more than 50 majority opinions; the text cites 84 justices (p.23). Unit of analysis: document (review or majority opinion), aggregated to justice-level means.
extraction.method: Minimally-supervised dictionary construction. (1) Train GloVe word vectors (text2vec in R) on the corpus: 300 dimensions, Xmax = 10, context window 50 tokens, drop the 20 most frequent tokens, tokens in more than 90% of documents, and tokens appearing fewer than 90 times, with AdaGrad (p.6-9). (2) Seeds: 10 uncontroversial positive terms (e.g., "superb", "brilliant", "great") and 10 negative terms (e.g., "bad", "awful", "horrible") (fn.3, p.7). (3) Extract the top 500 positive and top 500 negative words by cosine similarity to the seed-sum vectors, removing SMART stop words and AFINN opposite-valence terms (fn.4, p.7-9). (4) Weight token counts by tf-idf and by cosine similarity to get similarity-weighted positive and negative counts (Wp, Wn). (5) Polarity = (sum Wp - sum Wn) / (sum Wp + sum Wn), centered and scaled for comparison (fn.6, p.8). Accuracy uses a zero cutpoint. Sensitivity tests: corpus size (Figure 2), number of extracted words (appendix), and temporal re-estimation. Validity: benchmark accuracy against assigned ratings (with comparison to LIWC, AFINN, and supervised baselines in Table 1), convergent validity (polarity vs. number of dissenting votes, Figure 3), and discriminant validity (justice-level differences from LIWC and AFINN, Figures 4-5).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper is a measurement-validity paper. Validity is assessed by (a) classification accuracy against the benchmark review ratings, in-sample and on a held-out 25,000-review set; (b) convergent validity with voting divisions (number of dissenting votes); and (c) discriminant validity against LIWC and AFINN justice-level estimates and against historical narratives. The Supreme Court validity evidence is described as "suggestive - though not conclusive" (p.25).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language movie reviews from IMDB (benchmark), and all U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions available from justia.com for 1792-2010 (about 26,000 opinions). Institution: the U.S. Supreme Court. Era: 1792-2010, split into pre-1891 (Evarts Act), 1891-1925 (Judges Act and the start of the consensus norm's decline), and post-1925 windows (p.19-20). Claims are limited to document-level polarity. The paper says the method is not a universal substitute for supervised learning (p.15).

key_findings.finding: Corpus-based dictionary polarity classifies movie reviews more accurately than standard dictionaries. In-sample accuracy is 80.4% (12,004 negative, 12,663 positive, 332 neutral) versus 69.4% for LIWC (with scaling) and 71.3% for AFINN.
key_findings.numbers: 80.4% vs 69.4% (LIWC) vs 71.3% (AFINN); 12,004 neg / 12,663 pos / 332 neutral

key_findings.finding: Out-of-sample (held-out 25,000 reviews) accuracy is consistent with in-sample accuracy: 79.5% for the corpus-based approach, 69.7% for LIWC, and 70.6% for AFINN.
key_findings.numbers: 79.5% (ours, held-out) vs 69.7% (LIWC) vs 70.6% (AFINN)

key_findings.finding: Accuracy gains hold across corpus sizes. Even 5,000-document corpora beat the LIWC and AFINN accuracy figures, and accuracy approaches standard machine-learning levels by about 15,000 documents. Accuracy rises with corpus size, with diminishing returns after about 30,000.
key_findings.numbers: 5,000 docs beats 69.4%/71.3%; ~15,000 docs reaches roughly 80%; mean review 184 tokens (max 2,085)

key_findings.finding: Compared with supervised classifiers on the same movie-review benchmark, the approach matches Naive Bayes, MaxEnt, and SVM (about 79-80%) but falls short of Pang and Lee (2004, 87.15%) and Maas et al. (2011, 88.05%). The paper stresses it uses no classification labels.
key_findings.numbers: Ours 80.4; Pang, Lee and Vaithyanathan (2002) NB 79.7, MaxEnt 79.7, SVM 79.4 (mean); Pang and Lee 2004 87.15; Maas et al. 2011 88.05

key_findings.finding: Dictionaries estimated on temporal subsets of the Court's opinions differ sharply. Only 34.0% of negative and 27.7% of positive terms carry over from the early Court to the turn-of-century Court; only 24.2% of negative and 19.6% of positive terms carry over from the turn-of-century Court to the modern Court.
key_findings.numbers: 34.0% neg / 27.7% pos (early to turn-of-century); 24.2% neg / 19.6% pos (turn-of-century to modern)

key_findings.finding: Convergent validity: only the corpus-based polarity measure declines consistently as the number of dissenting votes rises. LIWC and AFINN show increases in polarity at various points, most notably in 6-3 decisions. In the modern era, the corpus-based measure treats unanimous opinions as generally positive.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative pattern across dissent counts; no coefficient reported

key_findings.finding: Discriminant validity: the corpus-based justice-level polarity is only moderately correlated with LIWC and AFINN. The Spearman rank correlation between LIWC and AFINN is 0.64, but the corpus-based measure correlates 0.29 with LIWC and 0.16 with AFINN. The standard deviation of justice-level mean polarity is 0.25 (ours), 0.22 (LIWC), and 0.16 (AFINN).
key_findings.numbers: rho(LIWC,AFINN)=0.64; rho(ours,LIWC)=0.29; rho(ours,AFINN)=0.16; SD 0.25 / 0.22 / 0.16

key_findings.finding: Divergence between the corpus-based measure and LIWC/AFINN shows an inflection at 1925. The paper treats this as the point after which the measures diverge less.
key_findings.numbers: Inflection around 1925 (no coefficient reported)

key_findings.finding: Justice-level examples: Harold Burton ranks as the most positive justice in the corpus-based measure, while AFINN ranks him 14th of 84 and LIWC 50th. The corpus-based measure gives Chief Justice White a substantial drop in polarity. Chief Justice Waite is marginally negative in the corpus-based measure, versus marginally positive in LIWC. Chief Justice Taney wrote significantly more negative majority opinions than under either comparison dictionary. Historical narratives are cited as support, but the paper calls the evidence suggestive rather than conclusive.
key_findings.numbers: Burton: 1st (ours) vs 14th of 84 (AFINN) and 50th (LIWC)

key_findings.finding: Sample scale: about 26,000 majority opinions across 217 years, averaging 2,097 tokens per opinion, which the paper calls longer than the longest movie review.
key_findings.numbers: ~26,000 opinions; 217 years; mean 2,097 tokens

limitations: Not a substitute for supervised learning when labeled benchmarks exist; the paper says it does not argue for universal replacement (p.15).
Measurement is at the document level. It obscures which subjects receive sentiment, and it does not capture sentiment within documents, which matters for long opinions (p.27).
Generalizability to other specialized vocabularies is untested. The paper asks whether the method 'travels well' and flags within-document variation in sentiment-laden word use as a concern (p.27).
Dictionaries may include noisy non-subjective terms; the authors plan to adopt Pang and Lee (2004) subjectivity filtering in future work (p.27).

The Supreme Court validation relies on voting divisions, which the authors call an imperfect proxy because consensual norms mask disagreement, and on historical narratives; the paper calls the result 'suggestive - though not conclusive' (p.17, p.20, p.25).
Temporal splits (pre-1891, 1891-1925, post-1925) are chosen on theoretical grounds; the authors note rolling windows as an alternative for semantic-change studies (fn.14, p.19).
Accuracy is computed with a zero cutpoint, and neutral reviews (332) are excluded from accuracy; LIWC is reported with and without scaling (p.10).
Unlabeled reviews are retained in the word-vector corpus, which the authors describe as a conservative test (p.9, p.14).
Majority opinions only are analyzed; concurrences and dissents are dropped for comparability across eras (p.18).
Terms were not stemmed (fn.13, p.19).
The appendix (corpus-size and seed-set robustness, opinion-length density) is referenced but not in the PDF.

summary_md:
Rice and Zorn (2018, a PSRM revise-and-resubmit draft) argue that off-the-shelf sentiment dictionaries break on specialized vocabularies. Their alternative starts from 10 positive and 10 negative seed words, trains GloVe vectors on the domain corpus (300 dimensions, 50-token window, terms seen fewer than 90 times dropped), keeps the 500 nearest words on each side, weights counts by tf-idf and cosine similarity, and scores polarity as (Wp-Wn)/(Wp+Wn). On 50,000 IMDB reviews this reaches 80.4% in-sample and 79.5% held out, against about 69-71% for LIWC and AFINN. It needs roughly 5,000 or more documents before it beats them. On about 26,000 Supreme Court majority opinions (1792-2010), justice-level polarity ranks correlate only 0.29 with LIWC and 0.16 with AFINN, while those two correlate 0.64 with each other. The choice of dictionary therefore reorders the units. The paper calls its court validation suggestive, not conclusive, and notes that document-level polarity cannot say which subject the sentiment is about.

For Paul's system the sharpest point is Stage 5b. press_value = DEBATE stance sign x stock Lexicoder LSD2015 intensity. LSD lists "credit" as positive and "debt*", "charge*", "risk*", "oversight*" and "fraud*" as negative, and run_stage5.R scores every release with no masking of those domain terms. I ran a quick one-path check on 1,563 text-bearing releases (UNVERIFIED, per DE-062). It found the effect real but small: 4.5% of positive mass and 7.0% of negative mass come from those terms, the release-level intensity rank correlation is 0.953 with and without them, and the LSD net sign flips on 4.1% of releases. The legacy regex scorer cites Rice and Zorn for its polarity formula, but its lexicon is hand-weighted. Its corpus-expansion helper departs from the paper's parameters and was never run. The paper is a measurement template the press layer has not yet applied, not a reason to change rankings.

summary_issues: Wrong benchmark size: summary_md says 'On 50,000 IMDB reviews this reaches 80.4% in-sample and 79.5% held out'. The paper uses 100,000 IMDB reviews. Accuracy is on 25,000 labeled in-sample reviews, which sit among the 75,000 documents used to train vectors (the other 50,000 are unlabeled), and on 25,000 held-out test reviews.

Threshold wording: 'It needs roughly 5,000 or more documents before it beats them' is consistent with the paper (it already outperforms LIWC and AFINN at 5,000 documents in its sample sweep), but 'needs' reads as a hard threshold and should be stated as 'already beats them at 5,000 documents'.

Venue overstated: summary_md and ext say PSRM revise-and-resubmit. The text names no journal; it shows a July 20, 2018 date and a footnote about posting to the PSRM Dataverse. The R and R status comes from the file name and metadata only.

Abstract framing: the paper's abstract describes the court application as U.S. federal appellate court decisions; the body analyzes Supreme Court majority opinions. The summary's 'Supreme Court' is correct for the body; the mismatch should be noted.

Local LSD figures (4.5%, 7.0%, 0.953, 4.1%, 0.976) are presented as a check that 'found the effect real but small'. They are single-path, unreproduced, and should be labeled UNVERIFIED in the summary, not as established findings.
The paper's court evidence is 'suggestive - though not conclusive' (p.25); the summary states this correctly, and the bearings keep it. No change needed beyond keeping the label.
Paul-alignment claim that his position note for legacy-regex-scorer says Rice and Zorn is on disk but unannotated was not checked against that note in this pass.
gaps_exposed: No domain stoplist or masking before LSD scoring: 'credit union', 'interchange charges', 'NCUA oversight', 'debt' and 'risk' count as tone in every CU release (stage5_lsd.R:48-61).

LSD intensity on congressional press releases has never been validated against human-coded intensity; the only check was a 3-case smoke test. Rice & Zorn's three-part design (benchmark accuracy, convergent validity against a behavioural proxy, discriminant validity against alternative dictionaries) is a ready template.
No dictionary-sensitivity test for the Press pillar: LSD intensity vs a corpus-derived dictionary vs stance sign only, measured as Kendall tau on Press% and on the top 133.

expand_tone_lexicon() was never run, and the CU-relevant corpus (1,563 text-bearing releases) is below the ~5,000-document size where the paper shows gains. A viable corpus-based dictionary would need the full unfiltered press corpus as the unlabeled training set, as the paper does with its 50,000 unlabeled reviews.

Document-level tone cannot say which target the tone is about (paper p.27). The system already handles this by separating stance (DEBATE, two-hop), but press_value still multiplies a target-specific sign by a target-blind magnitude.

extraction.research_question: Can step selection functions (SSFs) and path selection functions (PathSFs) be extended to model habitat selection during movement at multiple spatial scales, and how sensitive are the regression coefficients and predicted resistance surfaces to (a) SSF vs PathSF, (b) scale, (c) paired vs unpaired prediction framework, and (d) GPS acquisition interval (5 min vs 60 min)?
extraction.theory: Resource selection functions (used vs available design; Johnson 1980 third-order selection; Manly et al. 2002). SSFs (Fortin et al. 2005) and PathSFs (Cushman et al. 2010) are conditional logistic models of movement selection; predicted relative probability exp(sum b_i x_i) is inverted to give resistance. The paper argues that movement-based selection can differ from resource-use (point) selection, citing Squires et al. 2013, Elliot et al. 2014 and Zeller et al. 2014. Scale of analysis is defined as the Pareto-kernel radius (ecological neighborhood), not data grain.
extraction.data: Ten pumas (Puma concolor), six female and four male, Santa Ana Mountains, southern California; Lotek 4400S GPS collars set to 5-min fixes, Oct 2011 to Mar 2014. Collar duration 9-71 days (median 29). Final dataset 75,716 fixes after removing 2D fixes with PDOP above 5 (individual range 1,650-18,464; median 7,147). Unit of analysis: used/available step (steps of 200 m or more, buffered 30 m) and used/available 24-h path (n = 315 paths, 12 start-hour subsets averaged). Land cover: CalVeg vector data at 1:24,000, rasterized to 30 m, aggregated from 25 types to nine classes (chaparral 45%, urban 19%, coastal scrub 14%, annual grassland 6%, coastal oak woodland 5%, agriculture 5%, riparian 3%, perennial grassland 2%, barren/open 1%). Pseudo data: the 5-min data subsampled to 60-min fixes. Study period 2011-2014; no sex-specific analysis (sexes pooled).
extraction.method: Multi-scale SSF and PathSF with Pareto-weighted kernels. 19 time intervals (5 min, 20 min, then every 20 min to 360 min); generalized Pareto fitted per interval with gpd.fit (gPdtest); kernel radius = min(97.5th percentile of displacement, maximum observed displacement), giving scales of 532 to 7,390 m. Available area for each step/path = mean land cover proportion across kernels placed along the step/path. Predictors = differences in land cover proportion between used and available (no intercept, response always 1). Simple single-variable conditional logistic models at each scale; multiple models using the weakest-effect class as reference; characteristic scale = scale with largest absolute coefficient in simple models; multi-scale model combines characteristic scales. Mixed-effects (random puma) conditional logistic models failed to converge, so glm was used. Model performance: 10-fold cross-validation (Johnson et al. 2006) with Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). AIC compared only within SSF and within PathSF (equal sample sizes). Resistance predicted in unpaired (pixel-only) and paired (pixel plus kernel context) frameworks; resistance = 1/probability, not rescaled. Acquisition-interval bias: 60-min pseudo steps and paths treated against 5-min truth; bias = mean absolute difference in coefficients per cover type, averaged per scale. Connectivity: CircuitScape current density between protected areas on either side of I-15 (Temecula corridor); top 20 current-flow pixels along I-15 compared across resistance models.
extraction.scope: Population: ten pumas with established home ranges in one fragmented, urbanizing region (Santa Ana Mountains, southern California). Dispersing animals were not sampled and the authors say results may differ for them. Era: GPS data 2011-2014. Land cover from CalVeg (USDA Forest Service 2007). Methods are presented as general for SSFs/PathSFs at any GPS interval; empirical claims apply only to pumas in this study area.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Inference rests on the within-animal case-control design (each used step/path is compared with its own available area, which is the standard conditional logistic set-up), plus two internal comparisons: (1) 5-min data as truth versus 60-min subsampled pseudo data for the same animals, to isolate the effect of acquisition interval; (2) paired versus unpaired prediction from the same fitted coefficients, to isolate the effect of prediction framework. Out-of-sample performance is assessed by 10-fold cross-validation with CCC. Cross-method comparisons of AIC are explicitly not made.
measures: Relative probability of movement exp(sum b_i x_i)
Resistance = inverse of predicted relative probability (not rescaled or truncated)
Conditional logistic regression coefficients per land cover class
Land cover proportion difference between used and Pareto-kernel available area
Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (10-fold cross-validated)
AIC (within SSF and within PathSF only)
Bias = mean absolute difference in coefficients (5-min vs 60-min), averaged over cover types per scale
CircuitScape current density (McRae et al. 2008, 2013)
Count of top-20 current-flow pixels along I-15 (road-crossing candidate locations)

key_findings.finding: Regression coefficients are highly sensitive to the scale of analysis. Annual grassland and agriculture change sign across scales. For PathSFs, urban coefficients range about -10 to -30 and chaparral about -4 to -15.
key_findings.numbers: PathSF urban -10 to -30; chaparral -4 to -15; 19 scales from 532 to 7,390 m

key_findings.finding: Pumas show multiple characteristic scales of response during movement, described as mostly bi-modal. Coarse scales characterize urban and agriculture; fine scales characterize the remaining cover types (annual grassland, barren, chaparral, coastal scrub, perennial grassland, and others).
key_findings.numbers: Scales 532 to 7,390 m; 19 time intervals from 5 min to 360 min

key_findings.finding: PathSFs generally produced larger-magnitude coefficients than SSFs. Characteristic scales also differed between the two methods for every cover type except chaparral, most for coastal oak woodland and riparian. Annual grassland was the exception to the larger-PathSF pattern.
key_findings.numbers: Differences in characteristic scale for all types except chaparral

key_findings.finding: Predictive performance (10-fold CCC) rose with scale and PathSFs outperformed SSFs at all scales except the finest (532 m PathSF was the weak case). Best SSF CCC 0.976 at 6,555 m; best PathSF CCC 0.992 at 7,390 m. The multi-scale model did not have the highest CCC but was close: 0.943 (SSF) and 0.982 (PathSF).
key_findings.location: Results, Model performance, Fig. 4 (p. 1326); Discussion p. 1331
key_findings.numbers: SSF best 0.976 (6,555 m); PathSF best 0.992 (7,390 m); multi-scale 0.943 SSF, 0.982 PathSF

key_findings.finding: Within each method, AIC decreased with increasing scale. The multi-scale model had the lowest AIC for SSFs; the 6,555 m model had the lowest AIC for PathSFs. AIC could not be compared between SSFs and PathSFs because sample sizes differed.
key_findings.location: Results, Model performance (pp. 1326-1328, Appendix 3 not in text)
key_findings.numbers: SSF lowest AIC = multi-scale; PathSF lowest AIC = 6,555 m

key_findings.finding: Acquisition interval bias: 60-min pseudo data produced a consistent 3-4-fold difference in regression coefficients relative to 5-min data. Bias was larger for PathSFs than SSFs. Some cover types changed sign. Annual grassland and barren were preferred in 5-min steps but avoided in 60-min pseudo steps. Coastal scrub, avoided in the true steps, appeared preferred in the pseudo steps.
key_findings.location: Results, Acquisition interval bias, Fig. 5 (p. 1328); Discussion (p. 1331)
key_findings.numbers: 3-4-fold consistent difference; 60-min vs 5-min

key_findings.finding: Paired-framework resistance surfaces are more heterogeneous, with a greater range and larger maximum values, than unpaired surfaces. Unpaired surfaces assign one resistance value per cover type regardless of context. In the paired surfaces, urban produces rings of high resistance on entry but low resistance inside.
key_findings.location: Results, Sensitivity of resistance surfaces, Fig. 6, Appendices 5-6 (pp. 1328-1330); Discussion p. 1331-1333
key_findings.numbers: Urban (19% of area) gives highest unpaired resistance; 91st-100th percentile identical across unpaired surfaces

key_findings.finding: Resistance values were higher for PathSFs than SSFs and increased with scale. The finest scale had the lowest resistance range, especially for SSFs. The authors attribute the scale trend to coefficients becoming more negative as scale increases.
key_findings.numbers: Finest scale lowest range; resistance increases with scale

key_findings.finding: Road-crossing candidate locations (top 20 current-flow pixels along I-15) differed between SSF and PathSF, among scales, and between prediction frameworks. Locations were more similar at the same scale across methods and frameworks than within the same method across scales, so scale is a major driver of connectivity differences. Pseudo-step (60-min) models biased crossing locations and missed middle-I-15 sites, and SSF models also flagged sites absent from true-path models.
key_findings.location: Results p. 1330 (Fig. 7, Appendix 7 not in text); Discussion p. 1331
key_findings.numbers: Top 20 pixels along I-15 per model

key_findings.finding: Authors recommend PathSF models over SSFs when a choice is available, and caution that resistance surfaces and corridors are sensitive to method, scale and GPS schedule.

limitations: Only ten pumas, with sexes pooled; mixed-effects models with individual as random effect failed to converge, so glm was used and individual heterogeneity was not modeled (p. 1325).
Only land cover predictors were used; slope, topographic ruggedness and roads, known to affect puma selection, were excluded to simplify the methods (p. 1332).
Study animals had established home ranges; the authors state results may not hold for dispersers, who may select habitat at finer scales (p. 1331-1332).
The inverse of predicted relative probability is assumed to equal resistance; the authors state no empirical evidence supports this (p. 1333).

Whether the paired framework is superior to the unpaired framework, or a hybrid, is unresolved; the paired surfaces may not capture absolute fitness costs, and the authors note concerns about rings of high resistance around urban areas (pp. 1328-1333).
Resistance surfaces were compared visually and by distributional summaries only; no method for whole-surface validation was provided beyond road-crossing locations (p. 1333).
Connectivity analysis is a single illustrative CircuitScape run in one corridor (Temecula / I-15) and was described as cursory (p. 1326).
Bias was assessed only at one alternative interval (60 min); the optimal acquisition interval for pumas was not determined, and a shorter-than-5-min interval may be better (p. 1332).
AIC cannot be compared between SSFs and PathSFs because sample sizes differ, limiting method-level model selection.
The scale of analysis is the Pareto-kernel radius, and the grain was held at 30 m; the effect of grain was not examined.
The 24-h path analysis averages over 12 start-time subsets rather than estimating a single model.
Brownian bridge alternatives were suggested but not tested (p. 1333).

short_quotes.quote: Regression coefficients were extremely sensitive to scale and pumas exhibited multiple scales of selection during movement.
Given our results, when there is a choice, we recommend PathSF models be used over SSF models.
a mismatch between GPS collar acquisition interval and species vagility may ultimately bias corridor conservation planning

summary_md:
Zeller et al. (2016) used GPS tracks from ten pumas in the Santa Ana Mountains (75,716 fixes at 5-minute intervals, 2011-2014) to fit two kinds of conditional-logistic movement model. Step selection functions (SSFs) compare each observed step with available alternatives. Path selection functions (PathSFs) do the same for whole 24-hour paths. Both were fitted at 19 Pareto-kernel scales from 532 m to 7,390 m. The predicted relative probability was inverted to give a resistance surface, which CircuitScape then used to locate road-crossing candidates on I-15.

Main results:
- **Scale.** Coefficients are very sensitive to scale. Some cover types change sign, and PathSF urban coefficients run from about -10 to -30.
- **Method.** PathSFs fit better under 10-fold cross-validation (CCC 0.992 vs 0.976 for SSFs).
- **Sampling interval.** Coarsening fixes to 60 minutes shifts coefficients 3-4 fold and flips some signs.
- **Crossing locations.** These change with method, scale and prediction framework, and scale is the biggest driver.
- **Unvalidated core step.** The authors say no empirical evidence supports treating resistance as the inverse of probability.

The paper has nothing on lobbying, legislators or political networks. It matters here only by analogy, and only in one place: the path-finding layer turns modelled tie strength or probability into an additive cost (-log p or -ln(0.8·strength)) and then takes the cheapest route. The paper is a close case study showing that this kind of probability-to-cost inversion is an assumption, and that the routes it produces depend on scale and sampling choices. It also gives a template for testing such costs: compare the routes actually used against available alternatives in a case-control design. The staffer-route search already labels its cost as "not a probability of access", which fits both the paper's caution and D-025. What it lacks is any used-vs-available calibration, which PathSF would supply if an outreach log ever exists. All transfer is analogical (animals on land cover, not people in organisations). Strength is weak throughout. This analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Resistance is set to the inverse of the predicted relative probability, exp(sum b_i x_i), and the authors state that no empirical evidence supports equating that inverse with resistance. The routes and crossing locations it produces (top-20 current-flow pixels on I-15) shift with method (SSF vs PathSF), with scale (532-7,390 m) and with the paired vs unpaired framework.
bearings.paper_location: Methods (resistance = 1/probability, not rescaled); Discussion p. 1333; Results p. 1330, Fig. 7
bearings.system_side: Route cost is a parallel inversion. Each hop costs -ln(0.8 x strength) plus a weighted uncertainty term, and bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 returns the minimum-cost route. The code already labels the score 'not a probability of access' and calls u 'not a probability'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Analogy only. In the paper, a fitted selection probability on a 30 m landscape becomes a cost. Here, hand-set exposure strengths between people become a cost. What carries over is the methodological warning: the probability-to-cost transform is an untested assumption, and route choice is sensitive to it. That supports the system's existing non-probability wording (D-025). It gives no evidence about which transform is right for staffer ties.

bearings.paper_claim: PathSF compares each observed path with its own set of available alternatives in a conditional-logistic case-control design, and so estimates cost coefficients from observed route choices. It outperformed step-wise SSF at every scale except the finest (10-fold CCC 0.992 vs 0.976), and the authors recommend PathSF when there is a choice.
bearings.paper_location: Methods (PathSF, used/available paths, n = 315); Results Fig. 4 p. 1326; Conclusions p. 1334
bearings.system_side: The component's open question is whether shorter or cheaper routes match successful real introductions in an outreach log. Its costs (HOP_FACTOR 0.8, uncertainty weight, 5-year staleness half-life) are assumptions, not fitted values. The module states its costs are 'not fitted success or friendship probabilities'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This only applies if an outreach log of attempted and completed introductions is ever recorded. Each used route could then be paired with Yen-alternative routes as the available set, and conditional-logistic weights could be fitted for the hop-cost components. Until then it is a design template, not evidence. Any fitted output would stay a heuristic score, never an access or introduction probability (D-025), and would need a single-look holdout.

bearings.paper_claim: Whole-path selection (PathSF) gives coefficients of larger magnitude than step-wise selection (SSF), and different characteristic scales for every cover type except chaparral. The road-crossing sites also differ between step-based and path-based models. Composing steps does not reproduce whole-path behaviour.
bearings.paper_location: Results p. 1326 and p. 1330; Discussion p. 1331
bearings.system_side: The recruitment chain is ranked by the product of independent per-hop cosponsor-kernel probabilities (Dijkstra on -log p, then pathReliability). chainHold multiplies the per-hop activeP values, with ASKM 0.07 treated as constant and unestimated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Loose analogy. The paper shows that animal movement along a whole path is not the composition of independent steps. Legislators recruited through a chain may likewise not act as independent hops. The evidence concerns habitat selection, not social asks, so it only motivates checking hop independence against observed cosponsor join sequences. It does not show that the product rule is wrong here.

gaps_exposed: No used-vs-available (case-control) calibration of any route cost: the staffer and recruitment path costs are hand-set transforms of strength or probability and have never been fitted to observed route choices or successful introductions.

No sensitivity report showing how the returned top route changes when the cost transform (-ln vs 1/p vs linear) or the tie-strength time window changes. The paper shows that the cost-surface and route choices can be the dominant source of route differences.
No test of whether multi-hop recruitment behaves like independent hops (step-wise) or like a whole path. Chain reliability assumes independence.
flags: Wording guard (D-025): the paper's 'resistance' and 'relative probability of movement' language must not be imported to describe staffer or recruitment routes as closeness, access or introduction probabilities. The current code wording ('not a probability of access') already complies.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Nothing to flag there.
All bearings are analogical, cross-domain (puma movement on land cover) and UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul's pathfinding notes call for learned heuristics, A*-style handling of unstable information, and dynamic replanning. The built staffer router uses heuristic 0 and hand-set costs. This paper does not speak to heuristics. It adds a caution Paul's notes lack: the step that turns a probability into a cost is itself an unvalidated assumption, and route outputs are sensitive to it. It also offers a way to learn costs from observed paths (PathSF), which fits his wish for learned components. His annotations are not stale here; they simply do not cover cost calibration. Paul left no markup on this paper.

related.why: The recruitment chain runs a most-reliable-path search (Dijkstra on -log p). Zeller shows that the probability-to-cost inversion behind such searches is an assumption whose route outputs depend on how the probabilities were estimated.
Both turn tie strength into path cost for shortest-path search. Zeller adds a way to fit that transform empirically (used vs available paths) rather than setting it by hand.
Lawande covers grid and waypoint path-finding algorithms on a given cost surface. Zeller covers how such a cost surface is estimated and how sensitive the resulting routes are to it.

backlinks.why: Both papers infer movement cost or access from observed movement rather than straight-line distance: Zeller estimates resistance to movement with step and path selection functions, and Esmalian uses trip time vs trip distance. Both are relevant to any travel-cost weighting in the Terrier turf planner.
